cards.def: Duke of Athens who doubts the lovers' "fairy toys," chooses the mechanicals' play out of courtesy, comments throughout the performance, refuses their epilogue, and at midnight sends everyone to bed because it is "almost fairy time."
Theseus's bride, who argues that the lovers' shared story has "great constancy," later calls the play "the silliest stuff that ever I heard," and still pities Pyramus in his death speech.
Master of the revels who offers Theseus a list of entertainments, warns that the Pyramus play has "not one word apt," and is overruled when Theseus insists on hearing it.
The carpenter who speaks the prologue, pausing in the wrong places so that Theseus says he "doth not stand upon points," then explains the roles of Pyramus, Thisbe, Wall, Moonshine, and Lion.
The weaver who plays Pyramus, breaks character to explain Thisbe's cue, stabs himself at "Ninny's tomb," and after "dying" offers the court an epilogue or a Bergomask dance.
The bellows-mender who plays Thisbe, kisses the wall's hole, flees the lion and drops her mantle, and finally stabs herself over Pyramus's body.
The tinker who presents Wall with loam and rough-cast and holds up a cranny for the lovers to whisper through, then exits when his part is "discharged."
The joiner who plays Lion, reassures the ladies that he is "Snug the joiner" and "no lion's dam," then roars and tears Thisbe's mantle.
The tailor who presents Moonshine with a lanthorn, a thorn-bush, and a dog, and who is told to exit when Pyramus cries, "Moon, take thy flight!"
The newly married young lovers who, with Theseus and Hippolyta, tease the play, noting the prologue's missing "stops," the speaking wall, and Pyramus's death puns.
The sprite who, in this edition's Act 5, Scene 2, first sweeps the dust behind the door, then stays after the fairy blessing to ask the audience's pardon and hands if the "shadows have offended."
King of the fairies who, after the mortals go to bed, leads the fairies through the palace to bless "the best bride-bed" and the three couples with consecrated field-dew.
Queen of the fairies who, now reconciled with Oberon, has the fairies rehearse their song "by rote" and, hand in hand, bless the place.
The tragic lovers in the mechanicals' play who whisper through a wall, plan to meet at Ninus's tomb, and kill themselves after a lion stains Thisbe's dropped mantle with blood.
